newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain's Ofwat lays out water pricing stall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain's Ofwat lays out water pricing stall.

text.p: Britain's water industry watchdog Ofwat on Monday set out its stall for the next price review in 1999, saying that there would be an initial cut in prices and customers should see 55 percent of any savings.
"This adjustment will further tilt the balance towards customers," Ofwat chief Ian Byatt said in an address to a business and academic meeting at Liverpool, north west England.
Byatt has indicated previously that any efficiency savings should be shared equally between customers and shareholders.
But he told the Liverpool meeting that current methodology indicated that savings should be shared out 55 percent to customers, 20 percent in taxation and 25 percent to shareholders.
He said that customers had already benefited from increased efficiency but urged companies to satisfy needs further.
"The best way to please the regulator is to please the customers," Byatt said.
"He is laying his table out...water companies now have to justify their stance," said Gordon Culfeather of Greig Middleton.
"It is not exactly reassuring but hardly unexpected," said Nigel Hawkins of Yamaichi.
Ofwat said in October 1996 that it would review prices in 1999, five years ahead of schedule.
Analysts said companies such as Thames Water, which has relied on low bills to represent benefits to customers rather than one-off payments, could be in Byatt's sights.
"Byatt is rounding on companies that haven't made high profile customer payouts," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
Thames shares were down 5-1/2 pence to 682-1/2 pence by 1240 GMT while Severn Trent Plc shed 7-1/2 pence to 707-1/2 pence and multi-utility United Utilities slipped seven pence to 660-1/2 pence.
Water companies have come under heavy public criticism since privatisation in 1989 for hefty dividends and fat executive pay packets.
Many have picked up on indications from Byatt to ensure shareholder rewards are matched by customer price cuts but their image remains dull.
Byatt has encouraged return of efficiency savings to customers and shareholders and said any such moves will be taken on board at the next price review.
"Justifying the company's position will be key to the price review," said Culfeather.
But analysts said water sector shares would be more vulnerable to the imminent general election than to the price review at the end of the century.
"The major issue now for the stocks is the election. The market is a long-term investor but a short-term thinker," the analyst said.
The ruling Conservative party, which lags the opposition Labour party in the polls, must hold an election by May 22.
Labour has been fiercely critical of privatised utilities although it has retreated from its old, nationalisation strategy.
Labour has also said it would look at regulatory regimes if it came to power and suggested setting up boards of advisors to make regulation less personality-driven.
"Byatt might also have had an eye on government changes. He wants to be seen as tough on utility excesses by any Labour government," the analyst said.
